{{Short description|Mathematical structure in non-Riemannian differential geometry}}
In [[differential geometry]], a field in mathematics, a '''Lie bialgebroid''' consists of two compatible [[Lie algebroid]]s defined on dual vector bundles. Lie bialgebroids are the vector bundle version of [[Lie bialgebra|Lie bialgebras]].

== Definition ==

=== Preliminary notions ===
A [[Lie algebroid]] consists of a bilinear skew-symmetric operation <math>[\cdot,\cdot]</math> on the sections <math>\Gamma(A)</math> of a [[vector bundle]] ''<math>A \to M</math>'' over a smooth manifold ''<math>M</math>'', together with a vector bundle morphism ''<math>\rho: A \to TM</math>'' subject to the Leibniz rule

:<math> [\phi,f\cdot\psi] = \rho(\phi)[f]\cdot\psi +f\cdot[\phi,\psi],</math>

and Jacobi identity

:<math> [\phi,[\psi_1,\psi_2]] = [[\phi,\psi_1],\psi_2] +[\psi_1,[\phi,\psi_2]]</math>
where ''<math>\phi,\psi_k</math>'' are sections of ''<math>A</math>'' and ''<math>f</math>'' is a smooth function on ''<math>M</math>''.

The Lie bracket ''<math>[\cdot,\cdot]_A</math>'' can be extended to [[polyvector field|multivector fields]] ''<math>\Gamma(\wedge A)</math>'' graded symmetric via the Leibniz rule
:<math> [\Phi\wedge\Psi,\Chi]_A = \Phi\wedge[\Psi,\Chi]_A +(-1)^{|\Psi|(|\Chi|-1)}[\Phi,\Chi]_A\wedge\Psi</math>
for homogeneous multivector fields ''<math>\phi, \psi, X</math>''.

The [[Lie algebroid differential]] is an '''''<math>\mathbb{R}</math>'''''-linear operator ''<math>d_A</math>'' on the ''<math>A</math>''-forms ''<math>\Omega_A (M) = \Gamma (\wedge A^*)</math>'' of degree 1 subject to the Leibniz rule
:<math> d_A(\alpha\wedge\beta) = (d_A\alpha)\wedge\beta +(-1)^{|\alpha|}\alpha\wedge d_A\beta</math>
for ''<math>A</math>''-forms ''<math>\alpha</math>'' and ''<math>\beta</math>''. It is uniquely characterized by the conditions
:<math> (d_Af)(\phi) = \rho(\phi)[f]</math>
and
:<math> (d_A\alpha)[\phi,\psi] = \rho(\phi)[\alpha(\psi)] -\rho(\psi)[\alpha(\phi)] -\alpha[\phi,\psi]</math>
for functions ''<math>f</math>'' on ''<math>M</math>'', ''<math>A</math>''-1-forms ''<math>\alpha \in \Gamma(A^*)</math>'' and ''<math>\phi, \psi</math>'' sections of ''<math>A</math>''.

=== The definition===
A Lie bialgebroid consists of two Lie algebroids ''<math>(A,\rho_A,[\cdot,\cdot]_A)</math>'' and ''<math>(A^*,\rho_*,[\cdot,\cdot]_*)</math>'' on the dual vector bundles ''<math>A \to M</math>'' and ''<math>A^* \to M</math>'', subject to the compatibility
:<math> d_*[\phi,\psi]_A = [d_*\phi,\psi]_A +[\phi,d_*\psi]_A</math>
for all sections ''<math>\phi, \psi</math>'' of ''<math>A</math>''. Here ''<math>d_*</math>'' denotes the Lie algebroid differential of ''<math>A^*</math>'' which also operates on the multivector fields ''<math>\Gamma(\wedge A)</math>''.

=== Symmetry of the definition ===
It can be shown that the definition is symmetric in ''<math>A</math>'' and ''<math>A^*</math>'', i.e. ''<math>(A,A^*)</math>'' is a Lie bialgebroid if and only if ''<math>(A^*,A)</math>'' is.

== Examples ==

# A [[Lie bialgebra]] consists of two [[Lie algebra]]s ''<math>(\mathfrak{g},[\cdot,\cdot]_{\mathfrak{g}})</math>'' and ''<math>(\mathfrak{g}^*,[\cdot,\cdot]_*)</math>'' on dual vector spaces '''''<math>\mathfrak{g}</math>''''' and ''<math>\mathfrak{g}^*</math>'' such that the [[Chevalley–Eilenberg differential]] ''<math>\delta_*</math>'' is a derivation of the '''''<math>\mathfrak{g}</math>'''''-bracket.
# A [[Poisson manifold]] ''<math>(M,\pi)</math>'' gives naturally rise to a Lie bialgebroid on ''<math>TM</math>'' (with the commutator bracket of tangent [[Vector field|vector fields]]) and ''<math>T^*M</math>'' (with the Lie bracket induced by the Poisson structure). The ''<math>T^*M</math>''-differential is ''<math>d_* = [\pi,\cdot]</math>'' and the compatibility follows then from the [[Jacobi identity]] of the Schouten bracket.

== Infinitesimal version of a Poisson groupoid ==
It is well known that the infinitesimal version of a [[Lie groupoid]] is a Lie algebroid (as a special case, the infinitesimal version of a [[Lie group]] is a Lie algebra). Therefore, one can ask which structures need to be differentiated in order to obtain a Lie bialgebroid.

=== Definition of Poisson groupoid ===
A '''Poisson groupoid''' is a Lie groupoid ''<math>G \rightrightarrows M</math>'' together with a Poisson structure ''<math>\pi</math>'' on ''<math>G</math>'' such that the graph ''<math>m \subset G \times G \times (G,-\pi)</math>'' of the multiplication map is [[coisotropic submanifold|coisotropic]]. An example of a Poisson-Lie groupoid is a [[Poisson–Lie group|Poisson-Lie group]] (where ''<math>M</math>'' is a point). Another example is a [[symplectic groupoid]] (where the Poisson structure is non-degenerate on ''<math>TG</math>'').

=== Differentiation of the structure ===
Remember the construction of a Lie algebroid from a Lie groupoid. We take the ''<math>t</math>''-tangent fibers (or equivalently the ''<math>s</math>''-tangent fibers) and consider their vector bundle pulled back to the base manifold ''<math>M</math>''. A section of this vector bundle can be identified with a ''<math>G</math>''-invariant ''<math>t</math>''-vector field on ''<math>G</math>'' which form a Lie algebra with respect to the commutator bracket on ''<math>TG</math>''.

We thus take the Lie algebroid ''<math>A \to M</math>'' of the Poisson groupoid. It can be shown that the Poisson structure induces a fiber-linear Poisson structure on ''<math>A</math>''. Analogous to the construction of the cotangent Lie algebroid of a Poisson manifold there is a Lie algebroid structure on ''<math>A^*</math>'' induced by this Poisson structure. Analogous to the Poisson manifold case one can show that ''<math>A</math>'' and ''<math>A^*</math>'' form a Lie bialgebroid.

== Double of a Lie bialgebroid and superlanguage of Lie bialgebroids ==
For Lie bialgebras ''<math>(\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{g}^*)</math>'' there is the notion of Manin triples, i.e. ''<math>c = \mathfrak{g} + \mathfrak{g}^*</math>'' can be endowed with the structure of a Lie algebra such that '''''<math>\mathfrak{g}</math>''''' and ''<math>\mathfrak{g}^*</math>'' are subalgebras and ''<math>c</math>'' contains the representation of ''<math>\mathfrak{g}</math>'' on ''<math>\mathfrak{g}^*</math>'', vice versa. The sum structure is just
:<math> [X+\alpha,Y+\beta] = [X,Y]_g +\mathrm{ad}_\alpha Y -\mathrm{ad}_\beta X
 +[\alpha,\beta]_* +\mathrm{ad}^*_X\beta -\mathrm{ad}^*_Y\alpha  </math>.

=== Courant algebroids ===
It turns out that the naive generalization to Lie algebroids does not give a Lie algebroid any more. Instead one has to modify either the Jacobi identity or violate the skew-symmetry and is thus lead to [[Courant algebroid]]s.<ref>Z.-J. Liu, A. Weinstein and P. Xu: Manin triples for Lie bialgebroids, Journ. of diff. geom. vol. 45, pp. 547–574 (1997)</ref>

=== Superlanguage ===
The appropriate superlanguage of a Lie algebroid ''<math>A</math>'' is ''<math>\Pi A</math>'', the [[supermanifold]] whose space of (super)functions are the ''<math>A</math>''-forms. On this space the Lie algebroid can be encoded via its Lie algebroid differential, which is just an odd vector field.

As a first guess the super-realization of a Lie bialgebroid ''<math>(A,A^*)</math>'' should be ''<math>\Pi A + \Pi A^*</math>''. But unfortunately ''<math>d_A + d_*|\Pi A + \Pi A^*</math>'' is not a differential, basically because ''<math>A + A^*</math>'' is not a Lie algebroid. Instead using the larger [[N-manifold|N-graded manifold]] ''<math>T^*[2]A[1] = T^*[2]A^*[1]</math>'' to which we can lift ''<math>d_A</math>'' and ''<math>d_*</math>'' as odd Hamiltonian vector fields, then their sum squares to ''<math>0</math>'' iff ''<math>(A,A^*)</math>'' is a Lie bialgebroid.
